Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Hemant Jerwal / Ext: Capt. Panigrahi
Question: No Loadicator onboard, how will you calculate ship stability manually

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: How to Control Methane Emission from cargo
Expected_Answer: Maintain surface ventilation for the first 24 hours after loading to clear methane gas unless self-heating is detected. Monitor gas levels (CH4, CO, O2) daily. If methane levels rise, increase surface ventilation. Do not use standard ventilation methods that force air into the bulk of the cargo.
Fail_Trigger: Confusing surface ventilation with through-ventilation, which provides oxygen to a fire and accelerates spontaneous combustion.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: Stowage as per the IMDG code
Expected_Answer: The layout arrangement of dangerous goods on or under deck, dictated by the cargo's hazard class and designated Stowage Category (A to E for cargo ships). It ensures dangerous goods are positioned safely relative to accommodation, machinery spaces, and liferafts.
Reg_Source: IMDG Code Vol 1 (Ch. 7.1) / SOLAS Ch. VII
Fail_Trigger: Stating that all dangerous goods can be loaded under deck; ignoring the specific segregation from accommodation spaces.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda

Expected_Answer: Categories A, B, C, D, and E govern where dangerous goods can be loaded on cargo vs. passenger ships. Category A allows ON or UNDER deck on both ships; Category E allows ON deck only on cargo ships and is PROHIBITED on passenger ships. (Categories 01 to 05 apply to Class 1 Explosives).
Fail_Trigger: Failing to specify that certain stowage categories completely prohibit dangerous cargo from being carried under deck or on passenger vessels.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda

Expected_Answer: Must guide escaping vapors vertically upward at a minimum exit velocity of 30 m/s to ensure efficient vapor dispersion. Vents must extend at least 2 meters above the deck and be fitted with flame screens capable of preventing the passage of flame into the cargo tanks during high-rate loading.
Reg_Source: IBC Code Chapter 8 / SOLAS Ch. II-2

Fail_Trigger: Failing to identify the P&A Manual or the IBC Code as mandatory statutory items for chemical tanker operations.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: Are hull stresses more in Loaded or Ballast condition
Expected_Answer: Hull stresses (specifically hogging and sagging Bending Moments) are frequently higher and more critical in ballast conditions due to heavy concentration of localized ballast water weight in specific tanks while cargo holds remain completely empty, driving sharp weight-buoyancy mismatches.
Reg_Source: Class Hull Construction Rules / Ship Stability Booklet
Fail_Trigger: Assuming that a loaded ship always experiences higher hull stresses than a ballast ship; failing to recognize severe hogging risks in ballast.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: What is GHG (Greenhouse Gases) regulations
Expected_Answer: Mandatory technical and operational frameworks designed to reduce carbon intensity from international shipping. Includes the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) tracking structural design efficiency, the operational Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) rating vessels from A to E annually, and the enhanced Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP Diary Part III).

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: Structural strengthenings on forward and aft regions
Expected_Answer: Forward region: Hardened against slamming and panting via deep frames, panting beams, panting stringers, solid floors, and thicker shell plating. Aft region: Strengthened against propeller vibration and steering loads using solid floors on every frame, stern frames, deep cant frames, transom floors, and bossing plates.
Reg_Source: Class Hull Construction Rules / SOLAS Ch. II-1

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: Collision bulkhead requirements and rules
Expected_Answer: A watertight bulkhead fitted forward to restrict flooding if the bow is damaged. It must extend from the keel up to the bulkhead deck in a single continuous plane, located between 5% and 8% of the ship's length (LBP) aft of the forward perpendicular (FP). No doors or manholes are permitted; only mandatory piping penetrations with valve control located on the bulkhead deck are allowed.
Fail_Trigger: Stating that a collision bulkhead can feature an emergency access watertight door; getting the 5% to 8% LBP positioning rule wrong.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: How will you prepare for loadline survey
Expected_Answer: Verify all weathertight closures (hatch covers, packings, cleats) are intact and operational. Check all air pipes and ventilators for free movement of automatic float valves. Test all scuppers, non-return valves, and overboard discharges. Inspect side scuttles, deadlights, freeing ports, and ensuring load line marks are clearly painted and welded.
Reg_Source: ICLL Annex I / SOLAS Ch. I Reg 14
Fail_Trigger: Failing to check the automatic closing floats inside air pipes or presenting damaged rubber packing on hatch covers during preparation.

A.1156(32) (Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification - HSSC).
Reg_Source: ISM Code Element 10 / IMO Res A.1156(32)

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: Conditions of freeboard assignment
Expected_Answer: The mandatory structural and safety criteria a ship must fulfill to be legally assigned a freeboard. Core items include: Adequate structural strength (Class compliance), minimum intact stability, secure height of hatch coamings, effective weathertight/watertight integrity of openings, presence of deadlights, robust freeing ports, and safe crew protection arrangements (guard rails/catwalks).
Reg_Source: International Convention on Load Lines (ICLL) Regulation 1-26
Fail_Trigger: Believing that freeboard is determined solely by deadweight or volume; failing to state that structural weathertight integrity is a prerequisite.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: High tensile steel disadvantages

Question: MLC explanation and what all comes in social security
Expected_Answer: Maritime Labour Convention 2006 sets minimum global standards for seafarers' working and living conditions. Social security protection must include at least three of the nine core branches: Medical care, Sickness benefit, Unemployment benefit, Old-age benefit, Employment injury benefit, Family benefit, Maternity benefit, Invalidity benefit, and Survivors' benefit.
Fail_Trigger: Failing to name the core social security branches; stating that MLC only covers basic onboard food and wages without statutory social protection.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Testing of crane and how to do test of crain of 20T SWL
Expected_Answer: For a crane with 20T SWL, the mandatory proof load test must be SWL + 25% (i.e., 25 tonnes). The test is conducted by a competent person using certified proof weights or a dynamometer, testing the crane through its full range of hoisting, slewing, and luffing at minimum and maximum design radii.
Fail_Trigger: Using an incorrect proof load calculation (e.g., applying the old "SWL x 5" rule); failing to state that the test must span the full radius and angles.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Boat Drill frequency
Expected_Answer: Every crew member must participate in at least one abandon ship drill and one fire drill every month. If more than 25% of the crew has been replaced at a single port, a drill must be conducted within 24 hours of leaving that port. Passenger ships must conduct these drills weekly.
Fail_Trigger: Stating that a drill can be delayed beyond 24 hours when more than 25% of the crew changes; missing the mandatory passenger ship weekly rule.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Lifebaot lowering requirment
Expected_Answer: Every lifeboat must be launched and maneuvered in the water by its assigned operating crew at least once every 3 months during an abandon ship drill. Free-fall lifeboats can either be physically launched or simulated launched at 3-month intervals, but must be fully free-fall launched at least once every 5 years.
Fail_Trigger: Failing to specify the mandatory 3-month operational launch frequency for davit-launched lifeboats in the water.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: critical period and why it is called critical period
Expected_Answer: The critical period during drydocking occurs from the moment the ship's stern takes the blocks until the entire length of the keel settles onto the blocks. It is called critical because the upward grounding force ($P$) at the stern reduces the effective metacentric height ($GM$), causing a maximum drop in initial stability ($GG_1$).
Fail_Trigger: Failing to identify that the loss of stability is caused by the virtual rise of the center of gravity ($GG_1 = P \times KG / W$) due to the docking block force.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: use of ground tackle
Expected_Answer: Ground tackle refers to the entire anchoring assembly (anchor, chain cables, shackles, swivels, windlass). Its purpose is to securely hold the vessel in a fixed geographical position in designated anchorages, act as an emergency brake to arrest forward momentum, or assist in maneuvering and pivoting in narrow channels.
Fail_Trigger: Restricting the definition of ground tackle solely to the anchor itself; failing to mention its dynamic uses in ship maneuvering or emergency braking.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Hydrostatic Draft,COF
Expected_Answer: **Hydrostatic Draft**: The true draft measured at the longitudinal position of the Center of Flotation (COF). It is the precise draft used to extract accurate vessel displacement and hydrostatic parameters from tables, unaffected by trim. **COF**: The centroid of the vessel's waterplane area about which the ship trims.
Fail_Trigger: Using the mean of forward and aft drafts blindly for hydrostatic data without applying the first trim correction when the vessel is trimmed.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Lifeboat falls requirment
Expected_Answer: Falls must be regularly inspected with a specific focus on areas passing over sheaves. They must be renewed when necessary due to deterioration, or at intervals of not more than 5 years. Standard wire falls must be systematically turned end-for-end at intervals of not more than 30 months if not made of stainless steel or equipped with alternative safety features.
Fail_Trigger: Stating that wire falls can be kept in service indefinitely past 5 years without class approval or physical renewal.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: while approching port grounding hoq will come to know and what all actions as chief mate
Expected_Answer: **Indication**: Sudden drop in speed, vibration, change in steering response, echo sounder showing zero under-keel clearance. **Actions**: Stop engines immediately, sound general emergency alarm, exhibit aground lights/shapes, close watertight doors, take soundings of all tanks/bilges/voids, sound around the vessel to determine holding bottom, check for pollution, and check internal stresses before attempting to back off.
Fail_Trigger: Suggesting an immediate engine full-astern maneuver to pull off the ground without first taking internal and external soundings or assessing damage.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Loadline inspection(Survey)
Expected_Answer: An annual endorsement survey and 5-yearly renewal survey ensuring the ship's hull, superstructures, and closing appliances maintain weathertight integrity. Includes physical inspection of hatch covers, packing, cleats, ventilators, air pipes with flame screens/floats, side scuttles, deadlights, freeing ports, and checking that load line marks match the certificate.
Fail_Trigger: Presenting defective or taped-over air pipe floats or damaged rubber seals on cargo hatch covers during a statutory survey.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Girting of Tugs
Expected_Answer: The dangerous phenomenon where a towing line becomes angled transversely to the tug’s centerline, causing a severe rolling moment that overcomes the tug’s dynamic stability, leading to an immediate capsize of the tug. It occurs when the towed vessel moves faster than or off-course from the tug.
Fail_Trigger: Failing to explain that girting is caused by the towline force acting perpendicular to the tug's longitudinal axis, eliminating its righting lever.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Preventative measures for Girting of tugs
Expected_Answer: Use a dynamic gog-rope (or bridles) to keep the towline centered over the aft deck. Ensure the quick-release mechanism on the towing hook or winch can be triggered instantly from the bridge. Maintain clear communication between the ship and tug master, and avoid sudden large helm movements on the ship when a tug is fast.
Fail_Trigger: Failing to mention the quick-release mechanism or the use of a gog-rope as primary safety tools to counter girting forces.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Terminal asked you how much cargo can you take (with cargo capacity challenges and units)
Expected_Answer: I will calculate the maximum permissible cargo intake using the formula: Cargo = Total Displacement - (Lightship + Constants + Fresh Water + Fuel Oil + Diesel Oil + Lube Oil + Provision Allowances). Total Displacement is determined by extracting the maximum draft allowed for the current Load Line Zone from the hydrostatic tables. I will state the final cargo figure strictly in **Metric Tonnes (MT)**, cross-checking it against the volume capacity of the cargo holds in **Cubic Meters ($m^3$)** using the cargo's Stowage Factor to avoid a volume-bound or draft-bound error.
Reg_Source: International Convention on Load Lines / IMSBC Code / Grain Code
Fail_Trigger: Stating cargo quantity in a generic volume/weight unit without distinguishing metric tonnes from cubic meters; failing to account for ballast/fuel deadweight.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: C class division and how u will know where to put A class where b where c
Expected_Answer: **C Class Divisions** are constructed of approved non-combustible materials. They do not need to meet any requirements relative to the passage of smoke and flame, nor any temperature rise limits. To know where to place A, B, or C class divisions, I will consult the ship’s Class-approved **Fire Control Plan (FCP)** and the structural cross-sectional fire integrity tables in SOLAS, which dictate boundaries based on the spaces' fire risk (e.g., separating a high-risk Machinery Space with 'A-60' vs. low-risk accommodation corridors with 'B' or 'C' class).
Fail_Trigger: Stating that a C-class division must withstand heat for a specific duration; failing to use the Fire Control Plan as the definitive operational authority.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Inspection/maintenance of blocks
Expected_Answer: Blocks must be thoroughly examined by a competent person once every 12 months. Maintenance involves: 1. Checking the sheave for free rotation and excessive lateral play, 2. Inspecting the pin, swivel hook, and shackle for wear, distortion, or fractures, 3. Ensuring lubrication channels are clear and greased, 4. Verifying that the stamped SWL/ID number matches the Chain Register, and 5. Conducting a non-destructive test (NDT/Magnetic Particle) or checking for elongation if wear exceeds 10% of design dimensions.
Fail_Trigger: Overlooking the 10% wear limit on the hook/pin assembly; failing to cross-reference the physical block stamp with the official Chain Register.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: SMC - 6 implementation procedure/requirement, atleast tell me some
Expected_Answer: To issue a Safety Management Certificate (SMC), the vessel must execute these 6 core implementation requirements: 1. The company must hold a valid Document of Compliance (DOC) relevant to that ship type, 2. The shipboard SMS must be fully operational for at least 3 months, 3. An internal audit must be conducted and documented by the company, 4. All statutory and class certificates must be valid, 5. The Master and crew must demonstrate comprehensive familiarity with SMS safety/emergency checklists, and 6. Mandatory emergency drill frequencies must be strictly maintained and recorded in the logs.
Fail_Trigger: Stating that an SMC can be issued to a ship whose management company does not possess a valid, ship-specific Document of Compliance (DOC).

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Annex 1 machinery space dischg criteria, can u do in special area
Expected_Answer: Discharge of machinery space oily mixtures within a Special Area is strictly prohibited unless: 1. The ship is en route, 2. The oily mixture is processed through an approved 15 ppm bilge separator, 3. The oil content of the effluent without dilution does not exceed 15 parts per million (ppm), 4. The system is equipped with an automatic stopping device to halt discharge instantly if the 15 ppm threshold is breached, and 5. The mixture does not originate from cargo pump-room bilges or contain cargo oil residues.
Fail_Trigger: Failing to explicitly state the requirement for an active 'automatic stopping device' to operate inside a designated Special Area.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Social responsibility
Expected_Answer: As Chief Mate, Social Responsibility under MLC 2006 means safeguarding the seafarer's right to a safe and secure workplace, fair terms of employment, decent living and working conditions, health protection, medical care, welfare measures, and access to active social security protection. This includes preventing workplace harassment/bullying, monitoring fatigue limits, ensuring nutritional food standard compliance, and maintaining clear, open grievance redressal channels on board.
Fail_Trigger: Treating social responsibility strictly as personal courtesy; omitting its statutory framework under MLC 2006 regarding working and living rights.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Anchor dragging engine immobilised action
Expected_Answer: 1. Call Master, sound the General Emergency Alarm, inform the Engine Room, and notify VTS/nearby vessels via VHF. 2. Pay out more anchor cable (increase scope) to improve holding power, or prepare to drop the second anchor (veer walking back). 3. Order the crew to standby forward with emergency axes/cutting gear to slip the anchor cable if immediate collision/grounding is imminent. 4. Display 'Not Under Command' (NUC) lights/shapes. 5. Monitor the vessel's track on radar/GPS. 6. Prepare emergency towing arrangements aft or request immediate salvage tug assistance from VTS.
Reg_Source: Bridge Procedures Guide (BPG) Emergency Checklist / COLREG Rule 27
Fail_Trigger: Failing to immediately notify VTS/nearby ships; attempting to winch in a heavily dragging anchor using an immobilized or unpowered windlass system.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: COLREG Rule 7 Risk of Collision assessment
Expected_Answer: Risk of collision exists if the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change. Every vessel must use all available means appropriate to the prevailing circumstances and conditions to determine if risk exists. If there is any doubt, such risk shall be deemed to exist. Assumptions must not be made on the basis of scanty information, especially scanty radar information.
Fail_Trigger: Failing to state that the presence of a steady or constant compass bearing with a decreasing range is the primary indicator of a risk of collision.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: COLREG Rule 9 Narrow Channel operational constraints
Expected_Answer: Vessels proceeding along the course of a narrow channel or fairway must keep as near to the outer limit of the channel which lies on their starboard side as is safe and practicable. A vessel of less than 20 meters in length or a sailing vessel must not impede the passage of a vessel which can safely navigate only within a narrow channel or fairway. Avoid crossing if it impedes the passage of a navigating vessel.
Fail_Trigger: Suggesting a vessel should stay in the center or on the port side of a narrow channel; failing to realize that a crossing vessel must not impede transit traffic.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: COLREG Rule 17 Action by Stand-on Vessel limits
Expected_Answer: The stand-on vessel must maintain her course and speed. She *may* take action to avoid collision by her maneuver alone as soon as it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action. She *shall* take action (the 'extremis' clause) when collision cannot be avoided by the action of the give-way vessel alone. A power-driven vessel altering course in a crossing situation to avoid collision with another power-driven vessel must not alter course to port for a vessel on her own port side.
Fail_Trigger: Stating that the stand-on vessel can arbitrarily alter course immediately without waiting for the give-way vessel to fail, or turning to port in a crossing close-quarters situation.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: COLREG Rule 19 Conduct of vessels in restricted visibility
Expected_Answer: Applies to vessels not in sight of one another when navigating in or near an area of restricted visibility. Every vessel must proceed at a safe speed adapted to the prevailing circumstances. A power-driven vessel must have her engines ready for immediate maneuver. Except where it has been determined that a risk of collision does not exist, every vessel which hears apparently forward of her beam the fog signal of another vessel, or which cannot avoid a close-quarters situation with another vessel forward of her beam, shall reduce her speed to the minimum at which she can be kept on her course.
Fail_Trigger: Applying crossing, head-on, or overtaking rules (Rules 11-15) when vessels are not in visual sight; failing to maintain engines on immediate standby.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: COLREG Rule 29 Pilot Vessels identification lights
Expected_Answer: A vessel engaged on pilotage duty must exhibit: At or near the masthead, two all-round lights in a vertical line, the upper being white and the lower red ('White hat, red nose'). When underway, she must additionally exhibit sidelights and a sternlight. When at anchor, she must exhibit the anchor light or lights in addition to the vertical white-over-red pilot lights.
Fail_Trigger: Confusing pilot lights with fishing/trawling lights (Green-over-White or Red-over-White); forgetting that an anchored pilot vessel must display both anchor and pilot identification lights.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: ROR Card: Vessel Aground identification and response
Expected_Answer: **Lights**: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line, plus the mandatory all-round white anchor lights (one forward, one aft if length $\ge$ 50m). **Shapes**: Three black balls in a vertical line. **Sound Signal**: An anchor signal (5-second rapid bell/gong ring) preceded and followed by 3 distinct strokes on the bell. **Action**: If own ship approaches an aground vessel, verify under-keel clearance immediately, stop engines, and alter course away from the grounding hazard area.
Fail_Trigger: Confusing an Aground signal with a Not Under Command (NUC) signal (which has no anchor lights); failing to state the 3 distinct bell strokes for the fog signal.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: ROR Card: Sovereign Vessel (SV/RAM/Mine Clearance)
Expected_Answer: Sovereign vessels executing naval or specialized operations are classified based on their constraint status (often Restricted in their Ability to Maneuver or Mine Clearance). **Lights for Mine Clearance**: Three all-round green lights (one at masthead, one at each end of fore yard), plus steaming lights. **Shapes**: Three black balls or discs positioned similarly. **Action**: Stay completely clear; other vessels must maintain a minimum safe distance of 1000 meters from a mine clearance vessel.
Fail_Trigger: Failing to identify the 1000-meter mandatory safety distance requirement; confusing the green triangular mine clearance array with a standard trawler profile.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: MARPOL Annex II noxious liquid substances discharge rules
Expected_Answer: Governs control of pollution by Noxious Liquid Substances (NLS) in bulk. Discharges of residues (Category X, Y, or Z) are prohibited unless: 1. Vessel is en route at a speed $\ge$ 7 knots (4 knots for non-self-propelled), 2. Discharge is executed below the waterline via the approved underwater discharge outlet, 3. Distance from the nearest land is $\ge$ 12 nautical miles, 4. Water depth is $\ge$ 25 meters, and 5. The tank has been pre-washed as per the approved Procedures and Arrangements (P&A) Manual.
Fail_Trigger: Attempting to discharge any chemical residue while stopped or at anchor; failing to state the underwater discharge outlet requirement or the 12-mile distance limit.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Performance standards of speedlog and VDR
Expected_Answer: **Speed Log**: Must measure speed through the water (STW) for collision avoidance and speed over ground (SOG) for navigation. Accuracy must be within 2% or 0.2 knots. **VDR (Voyage Data Recorder)**: Must record and maintain data for at least the preceding 48 hours in a continuous loop. Capsule must include a fixed capsule, a float-free capsule fitted with an EPIRB-type hydrostatic release, and an internal long-term recording medium. It must capture bridge audio, VHF data, radar images, ECDIS displays, AIS, drafts, and engine inputs.
Reg_Source: IMO Performance Standards (Res.MSC.333(90) for VDR / Res.MSC.96(72) for Logs)
Fail_Trigger: Stating that a VDR only needs to record for 12 or 24 hours; failing to specify the dual requirement of speed-through-the-water and speed-over-ground.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Bridge visibility criteria statutory rules
Expected_Answer: 1. View of the sea surface from the conning position must extend from right ahead to 10 degrees on either side, and the blind sector caused by cargo gear or obstructions forward must not exceed 2 ship lengths or 500 meters, whichever is less. 2. Horizontal field of vision must provide an arc of at least 225 degrees (from right ahead to 22.5 degrees abaft the beam on either side). 3. The ship's side must be visible from the bridge wing. 4. Bridge front windows must tilt outward at an angle of 10-25 degrees to prevent reflections.
Fail_Trigger: Allowing a blind sector forward that exceeds 2 ship lengths or 500 meters; failing to know that bridge wing visibility must include a clear view of the ship's own side.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: Coming out of port steering failure action
Expected_Answer: 1. Engage the emergency manual override switch on the bridge steering console immediately to change to the backup hydraulic pump. 2. If response fails, command 'Stop Engine,' sound the General Emergency Alarm, and call the Master. 3. Order the Helmsman/Duty Officer to the Steering Gear Room to establish direct emergency local steering via telephone communication. 4. Exhibit Not Under Command (NUC) lights and shapes. 5. If headway threatens immediate grounding or collision, order the forward anchor party to walk back and drop an anchor to arrest the vessel's movement.
Reg_Source: Bridge Procedures Guide (BPG) / ISM Ch. 8 Checklist
Fail_Trigger: Attempting to turn the ship using engines before switching to the emergency steering gear system or failing to drop an anchor to stop headway when heading toward a hazard.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. R. Poswal / Ext: Capt. N. Nayar
Question: What happens when we sail in northern latitudes
Expected_Answer: Navigational challenges include: 1. Extreme magnetic compass unreliability due to the steep dip angle near the magnetic pole, causing high directive force loss. 2. Severe structural freezing and ice accretion, causing a virtual rise in the center of gravity ($KG$) and severe loss of intact stability. 3. Sub-zero temperatures causing structural brittle fractures if the hull is not built with low-temperature notch-tough high-tensile steel. 4. Extended periods of twilight or continuous darkness, poor GPS satellite geometry, and radar sea-clutter from pack ice.
Reg_Source: Polar Code / SOLAS Ch. XIV / Safety of Navigation
Fail_Trigger: Ignoring the stability hazard from ice accumulation on upper decks; assuming the magnetic compass remains reliable at high latitudes.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: Collision bulkhead requirements

It must extend from the keel up to the bulkhead deck in a single continuous plane, located between 5% and 8% of the ship's length (LBP) aft of the forward perpendicular (FP). Fail_Trigger: Stating that a collision bulkhead can feature an emergency access watertight door; getting the 5% to 8% LBP positioning rule wrong.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: How will you prepare for loadline survey
Expected_Answer: Verify all weathertight closures (hatch covers, packings, cleats) are intact and operational. Check all air pipes and ventilators for free movement of automatic float valves. Test all scuppers, non-return valves, and overboard discharges. Inspect side scuttles, deadlights, freeing ports, and ensuring load line marks are clearly painted and welded.
Reg_Source: ICLL Annex I / SOLAS Ch. I Reg 14
Fail_Trigger: Failing to check the automatic closing floats inside air pipes or presenting damaged rubber packing on hatch covers during preparation.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: Where will you get survey checklist
Expected_Answer: Extracted directly from the Safety Management System (SMS) documentation onboard under ISM Code compliance, which contains specific guidelines from the vessel's Recognized Organization (Classification Society) aligned with IMO Res. A.1156(32) (Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System of Survey and Certification - HSSC).
Reg_Source: ISM Code Element 10 / IMO Res A.1156(32)
Fail_Trigger: Stating that you will use a random checklist found online or made manually; failing to link the checklist directly to Class HSSC standards or SMS.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: Condition of freeboard assignment
Expected_Answer: The mandatory structural and safety criteria a ship must fulfill to be legally assigned a freeboard. Core items include: Adequate structural strength (Class compliance), minimum intact stability, secure height of hatch coamings, effective weathertight/watertight integrity of openings, presence of deadlights, robust freeing ports, and safe crew protection arrangements (guard rails/catwalks).
Reg_Source: International Convention on Load Lines (ICLL) Regulation 1-26
Fail_Trigger: Believing that freeboard is determined solely by deadweight or volume; failing to state that structural weathertight integrity is a prerequisite.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: High tensile steel disadvantage
Expected_Answer: Higher susceptibility to fatigue cracking under cyclic loading, accelerated degradation if protective coatings fail, lower elasticity (greater flexing/deflection under load), and highly complex, strict welding procedures requiring specialized electrodes and pre-heating to prevent hydrogen cracking.
Fail_Trigger: Stating that high tensile steel is completely maintenance-free or less prone to cracking; ignoring the critical need for advanced welding controls.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: Deck line
Expected_Answer: A horizontal line 300 mm long and 25 mm wide, permanently marked (welded and painted) amidships on each side of the ship. It marks the upper surface of the bulkhead deck at side, serving as the absolute baseline from which all statutory freeboards are measured down to the load line disc.
Reg_Source: International Convention on Load Lines (ICLL) Regulation 4
Fail_Trigger: Confusing the location of the deck line with the load line disc itself; stating that freeboards are measured from the keel up.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: Margin line
Expected_Answer: An imaginary line drawn at least 76 mm (3 inches) below the upper surface of the bulkhead deck at the side of a ship. It defines the absolute safety baseline limit for residual buoyancy; if submerged during progressive flooding, it indicates a catastrophic loss of stability and potential capsize.
Reg_Source: SOLAS Ch. II-1 Reg 2 / MS Act
Fail_Trigger: Stating that the margin line is located on the water line or exactly at the deck level; missing the critical 76 mm safety boundary parameter.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda
Question: General emergency alarm(he wants to hear where is it written 7 short 1 long blast)
Expected_Answer: The exact definition of the general emergency alarm (7 short followed by 1 long blast) is explicitly written in **SOLAS Chapter III, Regulation 6, Paragraph 4.2** (Communications: General emergency alarm system) and its execution requirements are outlined in the **LSA Code, Chapter II, Section 2.2**.

Surveyor_Name: Int: Capt. Daniel Joseph / Ext: Capt. Pramod Sharda

Question: Wind heeling criteria
Expected_Answer: The Weather Criterion (Severe Wind and Rolling) evaluates a ship's ability to withstand the combined effects of severe beam winds and rolling. The dynamic area 'b' under the $GZ$ curve above the gust lever up to the angle of downflooding ($\phi_f$) or $50^\circ$ must be equal to or greater than the windward roll area 'a' ($Area\ b \ge Area\ a$).

Question: which place will it recurve? At what latitude?
Expected_Answer: TRS tracks generally move west-northwest (Northern Hemisphere) or west-southwest (Southern Hemisphere). Recurvature occurs when the storm reaches the western edge of the subtropical high-pressure ridges (subtropical anticyclones) and gets caught in the mid-latitude westerly wind belt. Recurvature takes place at the **Vertex** of its trajectory, which typically lies between latitudes **$20^\circ$ and $30^\circ$ North or South**.

Question: why will it recurve
Expected_Answer: **Correction to previous answer**: Coriolis force acts continuously at all latitudes except the equator; it actually increases toward the poles ($F = 2\omega v \sin\phi$). It must be positioned aft of the forward perpendicular (FP) at a distance of not less than 5% of the ship's length ($L$) or 10 meters (whichever is less), and not more than 8% of $L$. 2. It must extend watertight in a single continuous plane up to the bulkhead deck. 3. No doors, manholes, or ventilation trunks are permitted through it. Only mandatory piping penetrations are allowed, which must be fitted with a screw-down valve operable from above the bulkhead deck.
Fail_Trigger: Failing to specify the 5% to 8% length positioning range or stating that a watertight door can be installed within a collision bulkhead.

It is strictly divided into four sections: Part I: Thorough examinations of lifting appliances (cranes/derricks); Part II: Five-yearly competent-person proof load tests and examinations; Part III: Thorough examinations of loose gear (shackles, blocks, wires); and Part IV: Heat treatment records. Every entry must be verified and signed by an approved competent person.

Testing limit switches, emergency stops, and brake operational clearances under power. 4. Question: 5. How do you calculate the metacentric height (GM) of a vessel practically?
Expected_Answer: Calculate Fluid GM = KM - KG_fluid. KM is obtained from hydrostatic tables using the true mean draft. KG_fluid is calculated by dividing the total Fluid Moments (Vertical Moments + Free Surface Moments) by the total Displacement of the vessel.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Pradhan (Int)
Question: Explain the variation in frame spacing along the length of a ship. Where is it more, where is it less, and why?
Expected_Answer: Frame spacing is reduced (frames are closer together) at the forward and aft ends of the vessel to resist high localized structural stresses. Forward spacing is tightest (not exceeding 610mm forward of the collision bulkhead) to combat pounding and panting forces. Aft spacing is reduced to handle propeller vibrations. Midships has larger, standard frame spacing because the structural forces (bending and shearing) are handled globally by longitudinal framing and continuous shell plating.
Fail_Trigger: Stating that frame spacing is completely uniform across the entire length of the vessel, or misidentifying midships as having the tightest frame spacing.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Sood (Ext)
Question: Differentiate between a Major Non-Conformity, a Non-Conformity, and an Observation during an ISM Audit.
Expected_Answer: 1. Major Non-Conformity: An identifiable deviation that poses a serious threat to safety of personnel, ship, or environment, requiring immediate corrective action or vessel detention. 2. Non-Conformity: An observed situation where objective evidence shows a non-fulfillment of a specific requirement, which must be resolved within an agreed timeframe (typically 3 months). 3. Observation: A statement of fact made during an audit that is substantiated by objective evidence, highlighting a potential weakness that could become a non-conformity if left unaddressed.
Fail_Trigger: Downgrading a major safety breach (like an inoperable emergency fire pump) to a simple "Observation" rather than a Major Non-Conformity.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Sood (Ext)
Question: What is a Class Status Report, and why must the Chief Mate review it immediately upon taking over a vessel?
Expected_Answer: The Class Status Report is an official, live document issued by the Classification Society detailing the vessel's current structural and mechanical health. The Chief Mate must review it immediately to check for: 1. Recommendations or Conditions of Class (which have strict deadlines for repair). 2. Due dates for statutory and class surveys. 3. Any continuous machinery survey requirements. This prevents the vessel from inadvertently operating out of class or missing critical legal deadlines.
Fail_Trigger: Assuming the vessel is fully compliant based purely on the physical certificates without verifying active "Conditions of Class" or "Memorandums" in the live report.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Pradhan (Int)
Question: You are ordered to anchor in an open roadstead with a depth of 90 meters. Explain your operational assessment, anchoring method, and scope of chain used.
Expected_Answer: At 90m depth, a conventional "Let Go" from the brake is completely prohibited; the massive kinetic energy will destroy the windlass or break the chain. I must use the "Walk Back" method. I will use the windlass motor to lower the anchor and chain all the way to the seabed (or 2-3 meters above it) before carefully controlling the final stretch on the brake. For a depth of 90m, the scope required is high (typically 8 to 9 shackles in good weather) because the catenary effect is significantly reduced in deep water.
Reg_Source: Admiralty Manual of Seamanship & Safe Anchoring Procedures
Fail_Trigger: Proposing to drop the anchor directly from the brake at a depth of 90 meters, or failing to state that deep-water anchoring drastically reduces the holding power of the catenary.

Verify trace heating on fire mains, fresh water lines, and air pipes is fully operational. 3. Switch to low-set sea suctions (or open steam injection lines to sea chests) to prevent ice crystal blockage. 4. Change engine room ventilation to recirculation mode to maintain ambient machinery temperatures. 5. Instruct the galley and medical officer to prepare cold-weather rations, thermal protective equipment, and anti-exposure gear.
Reg_Source: SOLAS Chapter XIV (Polar Code) & ISM SMS Procedures

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Nitin Nayar (Ext)
Question: Explain exactly how and when you will take a gyro compass amplitude. What condition is required for accurate calculations?
Expected_Answer: An amplitude is taken when the sun's or moon's true center is precisely on the celestial horizon. Due to atmospheric refraction, this occurs when the sun’s lower limb is about half a diameter above the visible sea horizon (or when the center is about 1 semi-diameter above the horizon). I will take a compass bearing of the body using the azimuth circle, note the exact UTC time, and calculate the True Amplitude using the formula: sin(Amp) = sin(Dec) * sec(Lat). Comparing True to Compass bearing yields the total compass error.
Reg_Source: Principles of Navigation / Practical Nav Tables
Fail_Trigger: Stating that the observation should be taken when the sun is physically resting directly on the sea horizon, ignoring the critical correction for atmospheric refraction.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Nitin Nayar (Ext)
Question: What is the specific functional purpose of soft iron spheres (Quadrant Corregiders) on a magnetic binnacle, and what type of magnetism do they correct?
Expected_Answer: Soft iron spheres are placed on the port and starboard sides of the magnetic binnacle to correct for "Sextantal Deviation" caused by induced magnetism in the ship's horizontal soft iron structures. Because this magnetism changes dynamically as the ship alters course or moves across different geographical latitudes, the spheres are designed to pick up an equal and opposite induced magnetic charge from the earth's field, thereby continuously neutralizing the dynamic horizontal error.
Fail_Trigger: Claiming that soft iron spheres correct for permanent B or C coefficients (which are corrected by permanent magnets, not soft iron).

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Nitin Nayar (Ext)
Question: Which specific type of gyrocompass does not suffer from a damping error (latitude error), and what is the exact mathematical formula for the damping error in standard gyros?
Expected_Answer: An "un-damped" or modern "controlled-type" gyrocompass (such as an Anschiitz gyrocompass, which uses fluid suspension and electromagnetic control to achieve settling without an offset) does not suffer from damping error. Traditional gyros that use a damping weight experience a North/South damping error (Latitude Error). The formula for this error is: Error = (D * tan(Lat)), where D is a design constant specific to the compass model and damping mechanism.
Fail_Trigger: Failing to name the specific compass design (like Anschiitz) or providing a standard speed error formula instead of the latitude/damping error formula.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Nitin Nayar (Ext)
Question: What are the critical meteorological factors that determine the formation and trajectory of a Tropical Revolving Storm (TRS), and what role does latitude play in the ITCZ forms?
Expected_Answer: TRS formation requires: 1. High sea surface temperature (>26.5°C) to a depth of at least 50m. 2. High relative humidity in the lower/middle troposphere. 3. Low vertical wind shear. 4. A pre-existing low-pressure disturbance. Latitude is critical because a TRS cannot form within 5° of the Equator due to the Coriolis force being zero. The Intertropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ) provides the necessary low-level convergence and cyclonic vorticity when it migrates away from the equator into higher latitudes during summer months.
Fail_Trigger: Claiming a TRS can cross or form directly on the Equator, or ignoring the prerequisite of a deep, warm ocean mixed layer.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Nitin Nayar (Ext)
Question: Explain the formation of an Oclected Front on a weather chart, and contrast a cold occlusion with a warm occlusion.
Expected_Answer: An occluded front forms when a fast-moving cold front overtakes a slower warm front within a mature cyclonic system, lifting the warm air sector completely off the ground. In a Cold Occlusion, the advancing air behind the cold front is colder than the air ahead of the warm front, forcing it to wedge beneath both air masses. In a Warm Occlusion, the air behind the advancing cold front is milder than the extremely cold air mass situated ahead of the warm front, causing it to ride up over the denser air ahead.
Reg_Source: Meteorology for Mariners & IMO Model Course 7.01
Fail_Trigger: Failing to explain that an occlusion represents the complete lifting of the warm sector, or reversing the temperature relationships between cold and warm occlusions.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Jordar (Ext)
Question: What are the primary hazards associated with carrying Coal in bulk, and what mandatory monitoring precautions must the Chief Mate implement?
Expected_Answer: Coal presents three major hazards: 1. Flammable gas evolution (Methane), which can form explosive atmospheres. 2. Spontaneous combustion due to self-heating, which depletes oxygen and produces Carbon Monoxide (CO). 3. Corrosion of structural steel due to acidic bilge water (especially with high-sulfur coal). Precautions: Monitor atmosphere in all holds daily for Methane, CO, and O2 before ventilating. For self-heating coal, apply surface ventilation only to remove methane; if self-heating accelerates (CO > 50 ppm), seal the holds completely and do not ventilate.
Reg_Source: IMSBC Code, Individual Schedule for COAL & SOLAS Ch VI
Fail_Trigger: Suggesting continuous ventilation for a hold where the carbon monoxide levels are rising, which supplies oxygen and accelerates spontaneous combustion.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Jordar (Ext)
Question: Explain the distinct hazards of carrying metal Concentrates in bulk, and detail the shipboard precautions required before and during transit.
Expected_Answer: Metal concentrates (e.g., Copper, Lead, Zinc concentrates) are Group A cargoes that present the hazard of liquefaction if their moisture content exceeds the Transportable Moisture Limit (TML). Liquefaction causes cargo shift, a severe reduction in metacentric height (GM), and potential structural capsizing. Precautions: Verify shipper's declaration and moisture certificates (<7 days old), conduct regular shipboard "Can Tests" during loading, inspect bilge wells to ensure proper filtering mesh, and stop loading immediately during rain.
Reg_Source: IMSBC Code, Section 7 & SOLAS Ch VI Reg 2
Fail_Trigger: Accepting a concentrate cargo for loading when the moisture content certificate is expired or shows a value higher than the certified TML.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Darodkar (Int)
Question: What are the specific operational and structural precautions required when loading Iron Ore Fines?
Expected_Answer: Iron Ore Fines are categorized as a Group A cargo (liquefaction risk). Operational precautions: 1. Strict verification that actual Moisture Content is below the TML. 2. Visual monitoring for any signs of splattering or fluid behavior in the hold during trimming. 3. Symmetrical loading across the centerline to maintain stability and prevent structural twisting. Structural precautions: Ensure total cargo weight per hold does not exceed the maximum allowable tank top load density (tonnes/m²) listed in the ship's stability booklet.
Reg_Source: IMSBC Code, Individual Schedule for Iron Ore Fines
Fail_Trigger: Failing to check the tank top structural load limits for high-density heavy cargo like Iron Ore Fines.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Jordar (Ext)
Question: During the loading of Sulphur in bulk, smoke is observed coming out of the cargo hold. State your immediate, sequential response sequence.
Expected_Answer: 1. Sound the general alarm, stop all loading operations instantly, and evacuate all personnel from the hold and deck. 2. Close the hatch covers completely and seal all ventilation systems to isolate the oxygen supply. 3. Do not use water to extinguish a sulphur fire in an enclosed space, as it generates highly toxic, explosive Hydrogen Sulphide (H2S) gas and highly corrosive Sulphurous Acid. 4. Boundary cool adjacent bulkheads with water. 5. If available, smother the fire by introducing fixed fire-extinguishing medium (CO2 or inert gas) or use fine sulfur powder directly on localized surface fires on deck.
Reg_Source: IMSBC Code, Individual Schedule for SULPHUR & SOLAS Ch II-2
Fail_Trigger: Proposing to direct high-pressure water streams directly into a closed cargo hold containing a burning sulphur fire.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Jordar (Ext)
Question: Your vessel does not hold a Document of Authorization (DoA) for carrying grain. Can you load grain under any circumstances, and can you load other cargo in the remaining spaces?
Expected_Answer: Yes, under SOLAS Ch VI Reg 9, a ship without a DoA can load grain provided it complies with the "Exceptions for ships without documents of authorization." The total weight of bulk grain must not exceed one third of the ship's deadweight. All untrimmed surfaces must be securely bundled or strapped down. Yes, other compatible cargo can be loaded in the remaining spaces, provided a strict stability calculation proves the vessel meets all standard grain stability criteria (e.g., residual GM > 0.3m, angle of heel due to shift < 12 degrees) and cargo compatibility rules are maintained.
Reg_Source: International Grain Code, Section 3 & SOLAS Chapter VI
Fail_Trigger: Stating flatly that a vessel cannot legally load any bulk grain if it lacks a formal Document of Authorization.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Darodkar (Int)
Question: Briefly define MHB. Which publication and specific section governs this classification?
Expected_Answer: MHB stands for "Materials Hazardous only in Bulk." These are materials that possess chemical hazards when carried in bulk but do not meet the criteria for classification as dangerous goods under the IMDG Code (Classes 1–9). They present hazards such as oxygen depletion, self-heating, toxic gas evolution, or severe structural corrosion. They are strictly governed by the International Maritime Solid Bulk Cargoes (IMSBC) Code, specifically defined and detailed in Section 1.7 (Definitions) and Appendix 1 (Individual Schedules).
Fail_Trigger: Confusing MHB with standard IMDG dangerous goods or stating that they are regulated primarily by the IMDG Code rather than the IMSBC Code.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Jordar (Ext)
Question: Name the three primary groups of IMSBC cargoes, define their characteristics, and provide one clear example for each group.
Expected_Answer: 1. Group A: Cargoes that may liquefy if shipped at a moisture content excess of their TML (Example: Copper Concentrate, Iron Ore Fines). 2. Group B: Cargoes that possess chemical hazards that could create a dangerous situation on a ship (Example: Coal, Ammonium Nitrate Based Fertilizers, MHBs). 3. Group C: Cargoes that are neither liable to liquefy nor possess chemical hazards, but still require proper stowage and distribution (Example: Iron Ore, Quartzite, Cement).
Reg_Source: IMSBC Code, Section 1.4 (Classification of solid bulk cargoes)
Fail_Trigger: Classifying Coal as a Group C cargo, or failing to identify Group A as the strict liquefaction category.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Darodkar (Int)
Question: To which specific IMSBC cargo groups does Coal belong? Explain the regulatory significance of its classification.
Expected_Answer: Coal is dual-classified as both a Group B and a Group A cargo (specifically under its updated IMSBC schedule depending on particle size distribution). It belongs to Group B because it possesses severe chemical hazards (methane emission, self-heating, carbon monoxide production, and oxygen depletion). It can also exhibit Group A properties (liquefaction risk) if it contains a high percentage of fine particles under 5mm size. Chief Mates must check both gas evolution and moisture levels.
Reg_Source: IMSBC Code, Individual Schedule for COAL
Fail_Trigger: Stating that Coal is strictly a Group C or only a Group B cargo, ignoring its potential Group A liquefaction hazards.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Jordar (Ext)
Question: As Chief Mate, how will you verify that the Transportable Moisture Limit (TML) value provided by the shipper is accurate and valid?
Expected_Answer: 1. Verify that the Shipper's Declaration is accompanied by a laboratory test certificate signed by a certified competent authority. 2. Check the date of the TML test; it must have been conducted within 6 months of the loading date. 3. Check the actual moisture content test date; it must be within 7 days of loading. 4. Conduct an onboard "Can Test" (shaking a sample in a conical can for 5 minutes) to check for fluid behavior or free water on the surface, which would invalidate the shipper's certificate.
Reg_Source: IMSBC Code, Section 4 (Assessment of acceptability of consignments)
Fail_Trigger: Accepting a TML certificate that is older than 6 months or failing to perform physical check-testing via an onboard Can Test.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Jordar (Ext)
Question: State the mandatory damage stability criteria that a bulk carrier must satisfy to survive a collision or flooding event.
Expected_Answer: Under SOLAS, the vessel must satisfy the following after sustaining assumed flooding: 1. The final waterline, taking into account sinkage, heel, and trim, must be below the lower edge of any opening through which progressive flooding can take place. 2. The maximum angle of heel due to unsymmetrical flooding must not exceed 15 degrees (or 17 degrees if no deck immersion occurs). 3. The residual metacentric height (GM) in the flooded condition must be positive (at least 0.05 meters) before accounting for free surface effects.
Reg_Source: SOLAS Chapter II-1, Part B-1 (Stability Criteria)
Fail_Trigger: Stating that the final angle of heel can exceed 20 degrees, or failing to know that residual GM must remain strictly positive.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Darodkar (Int)
Question: What are the legal operational conditions required for an Inert Gas (IG) system to be fully functional before cargo discharge on a oil/chemical tanker?
Expected_Answer: The IG system must maintain an atmosphere in the cargo tanks with an oxygen content not exceeding 5% by volume at all times. It must maintain a continuous positive pressure in the cargo tanks (minimum 100mm water gauge) to prevent the ingress of air during all stages of cargo operations, including discharging and ballasting. The system must automatically shut down if the oxygen content leaving the scrubber exceeds 5% or if the IG gas pressure drops below safe operational limits.
Reg_Source: SOLAS Chapter II-2, Regulation 16.3 & FSS Code Ch 15

Question: Define "Load Density". Where exactly on board can you find this value for your ship?
Expected_Answer: Load Density is the maximum allowable weight of cargo that can be safely distributed per unit area of a specific deck or tank top structure, expressed in Tonnes per Square Meter (t/m²). It is determined by the vessel's structural design and steel thickness to prevent localized structural failure or buckling. This critical value can be found in the ship's approved "Stability Booklet", the "Loading Manual", or explicitly mapped out on the "Ship’s Key Structural Capacity Plan".

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Vanamali (Int)
Question: What is the difference between standard Load Density and "Permissible Load Density"? How do you adjust it for deep-tank configurations?
Expected_Answer: While Load Density is the fixed structural design limit of the steel plate, the Permissible Load Density is the maximum localized weight allowed under specific operational conditions, which dynamically varies based on the height of the cargo hold, the draft of the vessel, and whether adjacent ballast tanks are full or empty (due to the counteracting upward buoyancy forces). The exact permissible limit must be calculated using the formulas and correction factors provided in the ship’s approved Loading Manual before loading high-density cargoes.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Nayyar (Ext)
Question: Explain the concept of "Strapping" a grain cargo. When and why is this procedure executed?
Expected_Answer: Strapping (or securing) is a mandatory method under the International Grain Code used to secure the shifting surface of bulk grain in a partly filled compartment (slack hold). After leveling the grain surface, it is covered with separation cloths or tarpaulins. Heavy wooden lashings or steel wire ropes are placed transversely across the surface spaced not more than 2.4 meters apart, securely anchored to the hull framing, and tensioned with turnbuckles to prevent any dangerous transverse cargo shift during a seaway.
Reg_Source: International Grain Code, Section 16 (Securing of Slack Cargo Surfaces)
Fail_Trigger: Suggesting that strapping is used for a "Fully Filled" compartment, or claiming that simple canvas sheets without rigid structural tensioning wires are sufficient.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Nayyar (Ext)
Question: What is Volumetric Heeling Moment (VHM)? Does a "Fully Filled" compartment have any VHM? Explain why or why not.
Expected_Answer: Volumetric Heeling Moment (VHM) is a mathematical representation of the potential shift of a grain surface within a cargo hold, calculated based on the geometry of the space and the assumed shifting angle of the grain. A "Fully Filled" compartment (specifically defined as Filled, Trimmed) *still has an assumed VHM*. This is because under the Grain Code, a standard 100mm structural void is always assumed to exist beneath the deck plating and hatch covers due to settling, which can shift and create a residual heeling moment.

Question: Explain the step-by-step procedure to find the total compass error using the Amplitude of the Sun. What is the precise timing of the observation?
Expected_Answer: 1. Take the compass bearing of the sun's center at the exact moment its true center is on the celestial horizon. Due to atmospheric refraction, this occurs when the sun's lower limb is exactly half a diameter (approx. 15 arcminutes) above the visible sea horizon. 2. Record the precise UTC time and ship's position. 3. Look up the Sun's Declination in the Nautical Almanac for that UTC. 4. Calculate True Amplitude using the formula: sin(Amp) = sin(Dec) / cos(Lat). 5. Name the True Amplitude North/South based on Declination, and East/West based on whether rising or setting. 6. Convert Amplitude to True Bearing and compare with the observed Compass Bearing to find the Total Error.
Reg_Source: Principles of Navigation & Nautical Almanac Calculations

Question: What is the specific purpose of the Flinders Bar on a magnetic binnacle, and what category of shipboard magnetism does it neutralize?
Expected_Answer: The Flinders Bar is a vertical soft iron cylinder placed inside a brass tube on the forward or aft side of the magnetic binnacle. Its purpose is to correct for the deviation caused by induced vertical magnetism in the ship's vertical soft iron structures (such as bulkheads, pillars, and stanchions). Because this induced magnetism varies dynamically with changes in the earth's vertical magnetic field as the vessel alters its geographical latitude, the Flinders Bar picks up an equal and opposite vertical induced charge to continuously neutralize this error globally.
Fail_Trigger: Claiming that the Flinders Bar corrects for permanent magnetic fields (such as Coefficients B or C), which are strictly neutralized by permanent corrector magnets.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Nayyar (Ext)
Question: Define the "Dangerous Quadrant" of a Tropical Revolving Storm (TRS) in the Northern Hemisphere. Why is it dangerous, and how do you navigate out of it?
Expected_Answer: In the Northern Hemisphere, the Dangerous Quadrant is the right-front quadrant of the TRS (relative to its direction of advance). It is exceptionally dangerous because: 1. The cyclonic wind speed and the storm's forward track velocity act in the same direction, generating the highest total wind speeds and monumental swells. 2. The rotary wind direction tends to drift the vessel directly into the path of the storm center (recurvature track). 3. The high swells slam the vessel from ahead, drastically reducing speed and steering control. Navigation Action: Bring the wind onto the starboard bow (45°), maintain course and speed, and make as much headway as possible into the safe semi-circle.
Fail_Trigger: Reversing the hemispheres or suggesting that a vessel should turn its stern to the wind when stuck in the dangerous quadrant of a Northern Hemisphere TRS.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Nayyar (Ext)
Question: What is the Damping Error (Latitude Error) in a gyrocompass, how does it occur, and how is it corrected?
Expected_Answer: Damping Error (or Latitude Error) occurs strictly in gyrocompasses that utilize liquid ballistic or damping weight systems to achieve north-seeking settling. As the vessel moves away from the equator, the earth's vertical rotation component causes the damping arrangement to exert a continuous, asymmetric torque on the gyro wheel, forcing it to settle slightly to the east (in North Latitudes) or west (in South Latitudes) of the true meridian. It increases proportionally with the tangent of the ship's latitude. It is corrected mechanically by shifting the lubber line/azimuth pointer scale, or electronically inside the master gyro processor using the formula: Error = (D * tan(Lat)).
Reg_Source: Gyrocompass Operational Manuals & STCW Section A-II/2
Fail_Trigger: Stating that a modern ring laser gyro or an un-damped, fluid-suspended Anschütz gyro experiences traditional mechanical damping weight errors.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Vanamali (Int)
Question: Name three major Warm Ocean Currents globally. Explain their general meteorological effect on coastal navigation and local visibility.
Expected_Answer: Three major warm currents are: 1. The Gulf Stream (North Atlantic). 2. The Kuroshio Current (North Pacific). 3. The Agulhas Current (South Indian Ocean). Meteorological Effect: Warm currents carry elevated water temperatures from equatorial zones to higher latitudes, heating the overlying air mass. This causes low atmospheric pressure, high evaporation rates, instability, and heavy rain or thunderstorm activity. Crucially, when warm, humid air blowing across a warm current meets an adjacent cold landmass or cold current (e.g., Kuroshio meeting the Oyashio), it triggers dense, widespread Advection Fog, severely restricting visibility for coastal navigation.
Reg_Source: Admiralty Ocean Passages for the World (NP136)

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Nayyar (Ext)
Question: Define Stowage Factor, Load Density, and Volumetric Heeling Moment (VHM). Explain how a Chief Mate uses them together to plan a bulk voyage.
Expected_Answer: 1. Stowage Factor (SF): The volume occupied by a unit weight of cargo (expressed in m³/tonne or ft³/ton), including normal broken stowage. 2. Load Density: The maximum allowable cargo weight per unit area of the tanktop or deck structure (t/m²). 3. Volumetric Heeling Moment (VHM): The volume of the potential void space shifted multiplied by its transverse distance due to an assumed grain shift angle. The Chief Mate uses SF to find the required hold volume, verifies that the localized weight does not exceed the structural Load Density limit, and uses VHM to evaluate the dynamic risk of capsizing under the International Grain Code.
Reg_Source: IMSBC Code Section 1.7, SOLAS Ch II-1 & International Grain Code
Fail_Trigger: Confusing Stowage Factor with Load Density, or failing to identify that exceeding the load density causes permanent localized deck or tanktop buckling.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Nayyar (Ext)
Question: State the three mandatory Grain Stability Criteria. Provide the formula to calculate the actual Grain Heeling Arm ($\lambda_0$) using VHM.
Expected_Answer: A vessel loading bulk grain must satisfy three distinct criteria across all stages of the voyage: 1. The angle of heel due to grain shift shall not exceed $12^\circ$ (or the angle of deck edge immersion, whichever is less). 2. The residual area under the Righting Arm (GZ) curve between the heeling arm curve and the GZ curve up to $40^\circ$, the angle of flooding ($\theta_f$), or the angle of maximum separation (whichever is least) must not be less than 0.075 meter-radians. 3. The initial metacentric height (GM), corrected for fluid free-surface effects, must be at least 0.30 meters. Formula: $\lambda_0 = \frac{\text{Total VHM}}{\text{Stowage Factor} \times \text{Displacement}}$.
Reg_Source: International Grain Code, Section 7 (Stability Requirements) & Part B
Fail_Trigger: Stating that the maximum allowable heel due to grain shift is $15^\circ$ ($12^\circ$ is the absolute legal threshold), or providing a standard fluid FSE formula for the grain heeling arm.

Question: What are the primary hazards associated with the carriage of Grain in bulk? Distinguish between its physical and biological dangers.
Expected_Answer: Physical Hazards: 1. Free-flowing properties that exert high lateral pressures on the structural bulkheads. Biological Hazards: 3. Spontaneous heating and rotting due to excess moisture, which leads to structural condensation (sweating). 4. Severe oxygen depletion and the evolution of toxic gases (Carbon Dioxide and toxic mold vapors) inside closed holds and adjacent spaces, posing a lethal risk to crew.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Vanamali (Int)
Question: Differentiate between a "Wet Shift" and a "Dry Shift" in bulk cargo management. What indicators identify each at sea?
Expected_Answer: A "Dry Shift" occurs when a dry, free-flowing bulk cargo (such as grain, coal, or small mineral particles with a low angle of repose) shifts mechanically across the hold due to the kinetic force of heavy rolling in severe weather. A "Wet Shift" (associated with Group A concentrates or iron ore fines) is an advanced, irreversible cargo shift resulting directly from liquefaction; moisture migrates to the surface, transforming a solid stable stow into a fluid slurry that sloshes to the low side and remains there. Wet shifts develop an immediate, progressive permanent heel, while dry shifts can sometimes be stabilized or re-trimmed.
Reg_Source: IMSBC Code Section 7 & International Grain Code
Fail_Trigger: Treating cargo liquefaction as a basic mechanical "dry shift," or suggesting that a wet liquefied slurry will return to the centerline when the ship rolls back.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Nayyar (Ext)
Question: Detail the timber deck cargo lashing requirements under the TDC Code. What is a "Hog Lashing" and when is it installed?
Expected_Answer: Timber deck lashings must be certified chain or wire ropes with an independent slip hook or turnbuckle. Lashings must be spaced not more than 3 meters apart longitudinally, secured to strong deck pads, and checked tightly throughout the voyage. A "Hog Lashing" is an internal, independent wire rope lashing system installed within the timber stack itself when the height of the deck cargo exceeds a specific structural threshold. It connects the port and starboard uprights or frames beneath the top layer of timber. It is tensioned to pull the independent structural sides inward, binding the inner core of the timber stack together to prevent the stow from independent shifting or spreading outward.
Reg_Source: Code of Safe Practice for Ships Carrying Timber Deck Cargoes (TDC Code)
Fail_Trigger: Failing to know that timber deck lashings require regular manual tensioning at sea because the wood shrinks as it dries out from exposure.

Question: You observe smoke emerging from a cargo hold while loading Sulphur in bulk. State your immediate command response and safe firefighting actions.

Do not use high-pressure water streams inside the hold, as this generates explosive Hydrogen Sulphide ($H_2S$) gas and highly corrosive Sulphurous Acid. 5. Introduce the fixed fire-extinguishing medium (CO2 or inert gas) to smother the fire, or apply a very fine, gentle spray of fresh water or sulfur powder onto localized surface fires if accessible.

Question: What is a Boat Note? Explain its legal and operational purpose during barge loading or anchorage operations.
Expected_Answer: A Boat Note (or Lighterage Note) is a formal receipt issued and signed by the receiving ship's officer and the barge master during lighterage or offshore anchorage transfer operations. It details the quantity, barge number, and any apparent discrepancies. Legally, it serves as an intermediate receipt confirming custody tracking; it does not replace the final Mate's Receipt or Bill of Lading, but it forms the essential evidence used by the Chief Mate to compile the final cloused Mate's Receipt.

Question: Explain the two primary types of venting arrangements required on modern tankers. How do they handle normal breathing versus rapid gas displacement?

Question: Detail the exact options available for securing grain surfaces in a partly filled compartment (slack hold) under the International Grain Code.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Martin (Ext)
Question: Explain the concept of "Statistical/Reserve Buoyancy". How does it impact the ship's survivability in damaged conditions?
Expected_Answer: Reserve Buoyancy is the volume of the enclosed, watertight spaces of a vessel above the load waterline. Statistically, it represents the potential buoyancy the vessel can draw upon when subjected to extra loading or flooding. It is critically governed by the assignment of freeboard. In a damaged condition, the loss of buoyancy in the flooded compartment must be exactly offset by the immersion of the remaining intact reserve buoyancy volume. If a vessel lacks sufficient reserve buoyancy, its margin line will be submerged, leading to progressive flooding and catastrophic sinking.
Reg_Source: International Convention on Load Lines 1966 & SOLAS Ch II-1

The Document of Compliance is issued by the Flag State Administration or a Recognized Organization (Classification Society) and is valid for a maximum of 5 years, subject to annual/intermediate endorsements.

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Martin (Ext)
Question: What are the explicit MARPOL pre-wash requirements for a Category X Noxious Liquid Substance (NLS) cargo under Annex II?

The tank must be washed using a class-approved procedure, and the resultant oily/chemical tank washings must be discharged entirely to a shore reception facility. The pre-wash operation must be continued until the concentration of the substance in the effluent to such facility, as verified by an independent surveyor using analytical testing, is at or below 0.1% by weight. The tank must then be fully stripped before sailing.
Reg_Source: MARPOL Annex II, Regulation 13 & IBC Code Chapter 16

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Sabyasachi (Int)
Question: Following the discharge of a Category X chemical cargo and completion of the mandatory pre-wash, state your management protocol for safe personnel entry into that tank.
Expected_Answer: 1. Mechanically isolate the tank completely (blanking lines/spectacle flanges) to prevent accidental cargo ingress. 2. Conduct continuous mechanical ventilation. 3. Test the atmosphere using calibrated, toxic-gas-specific detectors. Entry requires: Oxygen strictly at 20.9%, flammables <1% LFL, and chemical toxicity levels below the Threshold Limit Value (TLV). 4. Issue a formal Enclosed Space Entry Permit. 5. Station a trained standby person at the hatch with full rescue equipment (SCBA, ELSA, resuscitator, harness, and tripod) ready for immediate deployment.
Reg_Source: COSWP Chapter 15, SOLAS Ch III Reg 19 & ISGOTT/IBC Guidelines

Surveyor_Name: Capt. Martin (Ext)
Question: Differentiate clearly between the operating principles, gas detection capabilities, and precise use cases of a Tankscope versus an Explosimeter.
Expected_Answer: An Explosimeter (Combustible Gas Indicator) measures flammable hydrocarbon vapor concentrations in air from 0-100% of the Lower Flammable Limit (LFL). It requires oxygen to function because its catalytic filament burns the gas sample. A Tankscope (Non-Catalytic Volumetric Gas Indicator) measures the actual percentage volume of hydrocarbon gas (0-100% by volume) inside an *inerted atmosphere* (where oxygen is low or absent), utilizing a thermal conductivity sensor. Use case: Use the Tankscope to check if an inerted tank is safe for purging; use the explosimeter only during the final gas-freeing stages when fresh air is present.
Fail_Trigger: Using a standard catalytic explosimeter to measure hydrocarbon vapors inside an inerted tank, resulting in a false, dangerously low reading due to lack of oxygen.

Question: What are the primary structural and stability hazards associated with carrying standard Iron Ore in bulk?

If stowed incorrectly, it can exceed the maximum allowable load density (t/m²), inducing plate buckling. 2. Stiff Ship Condition: The concentration of weight low in the holds lowers the vessel's vertical center of gravity ($KG$), causing a massively excessive metacentric height ($GM$). This results in an extremely violent, quick, and snappy rolling period at sea, which subjects structural frames, mast houses, and lashing arrangements to extreme dynamic accelerating forces.
